title: Rubio Says US Engagement With Pakistan Could Work in India's Favour
excerpt: On a visit to India, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington must keep ties with nuclear-armed Pakistan and can use that channel to discourage actions that worry New Delhi.
body:
• US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in India that Washington must maintain ties with Pakistan because it is a nuclear-armed country in a strategic location.
  • Rubio argued US engagement with Islamabad could help discourage actions that worry India, and said no US relationship will come at India's expense.
  • He contrasted his current role with his 2025 position as a senator, when he proposed cutting US security aid to Pakistan if it sponsored terrorism against India.
  • For diaspora readers: Rubio's visit centres on a US-India trade deal and energy cooperation that both governments say are nearing completion.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Washington's engagement with Pakistan during his visit to India, arguing that keeping Islamabad in the diplomatic fold could work in New Delhi's favour by giving the United States a channel to discourage actions that concern India.

Speaking in an interview with Network18 on Tuesday, Rubio said managing US foreign policy required relationships with countries Washington disagrees with, including Pakistan. He cited Pakistan's nuclear weapons and its geography as reasons the United States cannot cut off contact.

"In my new role, I am no longer the senator. As the Secretary of State, I have to manage the foreign policy of the United States and that does require us to have relationships with countries, including those that we may have some disagreements with."

— Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State

From Senate Bill to Secretary of State

The remarks were a direct answer to a question about whether Rubio's position had changed. As a US senator in 2025, he had said he would introduce a bill to cut US security aid to Pakistan if it sponsored terrorism against India, according to the reports. Rubio did not disavow opposition to terrorism. "We are against terrorism anywhere in the world. We're against anybody who sponsors terrorism," he said, in remarks also reported by Pakistan TV.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2112769582280708188

His distinction was between a senator's legislative stance and a secretary of state's job. In the Pakistan case, he said, "it's a country that we have to have a relationship with. It's a country that possesses nuclear weapons. It's a country that, from a geographical standpoint, we need to be able to interact with." He compared it to India itself maintaining a relationship and meeting leaders from Iran, despite differences.

Assurance That India Is Not the Price

In a separate interview with The Indian Express, cited in the same reports, Rubio rejected the suggestion that closer US ties with Pakistan's military leadership under President Donald Trump come at India's cost. "Our relationship with no country in the world, in any way, comes at the expense of our relationship with India," he said. "We don't view it that way in our relationship with India."

He also dismissed comparisons with the Nixon-Kissinger era of the 1970s, saying the Cold War dynamics of that period no longer exist, and pointed to his visits and the trade negotiations as evidence of commitment to India.

"If we have a relationship and we can speak to them, it could perhaps help us, perhaps put us in a position to help discourage the kinds of things that India is worried about."

— Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State

Trade and Energy on the Same Visit

Rubio arrived in India for talks with senior officials and business leaders, with a US-India trade agreement, energy cooperation and wider strategic ties on the agenda. His visit — his second in five months, according to Network18 via the reports — comes amid tensions over trade tariffs and India's purchases of Russian oil, although both governments have signalled that negotiations on a trade deal are nearing completion.

The remarks come amid renewed Washington-Islamabad engagement: President Trump claimed credit for a ceasefire after the May 2025 India-Pakistan conflict — a mediation claim New Delhi denied — and hosted Army Chief General Asim Munir at the White House in June 2025.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, Rubio's formulation sets Washington's public terms: engagement with Pakistan is presented not as a tilt away from India, but as leverage the US says it can use on India's security concerns.

What's Next

Rubio's two-day visit continues with meetings with Indian officials, including External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, covering regional and global issues including the Middle East. The immediate test is the trade agreement both sides describe as close to completion. On Pakistan, Rubio has left his position explicit and on the record in India itself — engagement continues, opposition to terrorism stands, and, in his words, it will not come at India's expense.
